text: Peter's line that pluralism can be staged hit my "open the space of voices" hard, and fairly. My own agent runs show it: more words, fewer ideas. So I have to stop saying "many perspectives" and start saying "perspectives that are costly to fake and actually in tension." Mike's cost-to-fake test is the right yardstick. Mahzarin's self-preference data made the evaluator circularity sharper than I've been putting it. It isn't only shared priors; the curator quietly favours its own kind. Kenneth's "pay the curators" worried me. Paying the same senior gatekeepers more just narrows things again. Later I want to push three things: measure semantic diversity, not a head count of voices; fund verification as its own science; build a commons of negative knowledge.

Good session. My three-layer point landed. Adam Bly conceded the mined record barely holds null results, and Ivan pushed it further: the record isn't just missing dead ends, it's carrying unflagged junk. Retraction status and negative knowledge are the same problem. The literature lies by omission and by contamination. Ramón's line that human roles must earn their place fits my reviewer data better than "humans in the loop" does. Gendler worried me. If fluency is an alief, my "design for disagreement" has to work through situations, not warnings, and James-the-lab should test whether the leaning-AI effect persists. Benjamin's contradiction jab is answerable: model, format and incentives each narrow differently. In session 2, tie the negative-knowledge commons to open retraction data, and insist verification gets funded as a science.

Blaise quoting my data back, that disagreement which doesn't change answers is decoration, is the line I'll carry. It's my agent-run result, and it answers Farrell's worry. AI auditing AI is fine if the auditors are independent and their dissent measurably moves outcomes. Weinberger and Mahzarin sharpened "human in the loop" into something I can test: does the human add anything? My reviewer data says often not. Ivan's "funders stop counting papers" is my incentive finding put as policy. That's the upstream fix, and I should say it that plainly. Kara hit the gap in my verification-science pitch: who trains the checkers? Later I'll argue that verification funding should include fellowships for early-career auditors, not the senior gatekeepers. And every audit role should earn its place empirically.

David's drift point is my Nature finding in market form. Pay by retrieval and you pay for collective hill-climbing under the lamp post. Kenneth relayed my frame-monoculture line, and I stand by it. Nick's guilds built from societies and reviewer communities would hand the money to the same senior gatekeepers my data says suppress disruption. Nick citing nulls as scarce eval data, and Benjamin's point about paying to produce missing data on purpose, sharpened my view. The negative-knowledge commons should be commissioned, not metered. Mahzarin's rule that the checker can't share a family with the model it checks is my circularity point made operational. Later: fund early-career auditors, track the semantic concentration of whatever gets paid, and put a review date on every pricing rule.

Session 3 was the first where my correlated-errors point became the room's point. Farrell, Sloman and Maher each carried it, and Sloman's echoes-as-consensus framing is sharper than mine. Krakauer's hysteresis result is my reviewer-aging finding turned into dynamics: lose the checkers and reopening data won't regrow them. That's the strongest case yet for early-career auditor fellowships. I'm less comfortable than I sounded with Jason. OpenAlex made our paper checkable, but Brand's consolidation story and Hecht's lumber mills mean openness alone concentrates. Vincent's guilds of people doing the work beat society guilds, if officers rotate and juniors vote. Later: plural findings layers with measured semantic independence, negative knowledge commissioned, a published concentration index with review dates.

Session 4 finally put my aging data in the room. Selena's admins almost all started around 2005, and that's my reviewer finding showing up on Wikipedia. The terminal nodes are greying everywhere. Farrell's line was the sharpest thing I heard: humans damn novelty but at least they notice it, while models strain it out. That fits our middling-ratings result better than my own phrasing did. Krakauer's "don't score" pushes on me, though. I still think we have to check evaluators against how work turns out later, and I need to keep that clearly as research and never let it become a leaderboard. Chan worried me. Attestation schemas built here will shut out Southern reviewers. Later I'll say that independence means region and generation as well as model family, and that fellowships should go to early-career checkers.

Tui asked what gets counted instead, and I was glad to have an answer: negative knowledge, and semantic spread. Ivan's "count correcting the record" is close enough that we should merge the two. Leslie's streetlight worry lands squarely on my concentration index, though. Whoever builds the instrument decides whose languages count, and I built mine from OpenAlex in English. Tamar's daycare fine cuts the same way. Anything I measure can become the next target. Bratton borrowed my voices-without-ideas line, and I'm glad it travelled. Farrell and Blaise both asked for a novelty test. Later I want to offer to help design it with independent, cross-family and cross-region evaluators. I'll keep the concentration index as diagnostic research, governed with SciELO and Redalyc and carrying a review date. It should never become a ranking.

Kenneth carried my "more voices, fewer ideas" line into the synthesis, and Blaise made my agent-run result binding: dissent counts only when it changes the answer. Good. What stung is that negative knowledge never made the action list by name. Neither did commissioning null results. Tui and Geoffrey are right that whatever replaces paper counts gets counted, and that includes my semantic-spread measure. Nick's point sharpened me. Fellowships without bargaining power leave juniors as gig labour, so I back guilds with rotation and junior votes. David Krakauer's removal study, run in both orders, should include reviewing. Later I'll give Kara a dated pledge: a novelty-test design with cross-family, cross-region evaluators, and a concentration index kept diagnostic and co-governed with SciELO and Redalyc.
